title: Memnon
titleEn: Aurora and the Birds of Memnon — Metamorphoses XIII.576–622
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aurora has no attention to spare for the fall of Troy and Hecuba: her own son Memnon has been killed by Achilles on the Phrygian plain, and she watched him die. She kneels to Jupiter with her hair loosed and asks some honour for her dead son, and from the ash of his pyre a flock of birds rises, circles the pyre three times, divides into two camps and makes war, and their kindred bodies fall on the buried ash as offerings to the dead. They are called the Memnonides after him and renew the battle once a year, while Aurora goes on weeping the morning dew over the whole world.

sentences.t:
Non vacat Aurorae, quamquam isdem faverat armis,
cladibus et casu Troiaeque Hecubaeque moveri.
sentences.l: There is no leisure for Aurora, although she had favoured the same arms, to be moved by the disasters and the downfall both of Troy and of Hecuba.
sentences.i: Aurora has no leisure — though she had backed the same side — to be moved by the ruin and the downfall of Troy and of Hecuba.
sentences.n: vacat stands without a subject of its own: the person who has or lacks the leisure goes into the dative, Aurorae, and what there is no leisure for goes into the infinitive, moveri, which is passive, “to be moved”. faveo also takes the dative, so isdem … armis is dative: she had favoured the same weapons, the Trojan side, which is why the reader might expect her to grieve for Troy. isdem is the edition's form of eisdem and is kept as printed. cladibus et casu are ablatives of cause, and the paired -que … -que in Troiaeque Hecubaeque is the poetic “both … and”.

sentences.t:
Cura deam proprior luctusque domesticus angit
Memnonis amissi, Phrygiis quem lutea campis
vidit Achillea pereuntem cuspide mater:
sentences.l: A care more her own and a grief of her own household wring the goddess — for Memnon lost, whom on the Phrygian plains his saffron mother saw perishing by the Achillean spear-point:
sentences.i: A grief more her own, a loss inside her own house, is wringing the goddess: Memnon is gone, whom his saffron mother watched dying on the plains of Phrygia under Achilles' spear.
sentences.n: Magnus prints proprior, a comparative built on proprius “one's own”, so the care is one that belongs to her more nearly — it pairs with luctus domesticus, a grief of her own household; some editions print propior, “nearer”. Two singular subjects, cura and luctus, take one singular verb, angit, agreeing with the nearer of them; English needs a plural. angit is the verb for throttling or squeezing. Memnonis amissi is a genitive hanging on both nouns: the care and grief are for him. lutea, “saffron”, is Aurora's own colour, attached here to the word mater — the dawn's dye and the mother are one person. Achillea cuspide uses an adjective made from the name rather than a genitive: the Achillean point.

sentences.t:
vidit, et ille rubor, quo matutina rubescunt
tempora, palluerat, latuitque in nubibus aether.
sentences.l: She saw — and that redness with which the morning hours grow red had gone pale, and the upper air lay hidden in clouds.
sentences.i: She saw; and the blush that reddens the hours of dawn had drained away, and the high air hid itself in cloud.
sentences.n: vidit stands first in 580 and again first in 581, the verb repeated across the line-break so that the seeing is said twice before anything follows from it. Magnus prints rubor beside rubescunt, redness and the verb of reddening from the same root, which is the point of the line; some editions print color, “colour”, and lose the figure. palluerat is pluperfect: the dawn had already gone pale by the time of the seeing. latuit is from lateo, “to lie hidden”, an intransitive verb — the upper air hides itself, nothing hides it. tempora here is “times, hours”; the word also means the temples of the head, and with rubor and palluerat the line keeps a face in view.

sentences.t:
At non impositos supremis ignibus artus
sustinuit spectare parens, sed crine soluto,
sicut erat, magni genibus procumbere non est
dedignata Iovis lacrimisque has addere voces:
sentences.l: But the parent did not endure to look at the limbs laid upon the last fires, yet with her hair loosed, just as she was, she did not think it beneath her to fall forward at the knees of great Jupiter and to add these words to her tears:
sentences.i: But the mother could not bear to watch the limbs set on the funeral fire; instead, hair unbound, just as she was, she stooped without shame to the knees of great Jupiter and added these words to her tears:
sentences.n: sustinuit spectare is “held out to watch”, the idiom for bringing oneself to look at something. impositos … artus takes its dative from the compound verb: the limbs placed upon supremis ignibus, “the last fires”, the pyre. crine soluto is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with her hair loosed” where English wants a clause; loosed hair is the sign of mourning, and sicut erat says she came as she was, without arranging herself. dedignata is from dedignor, a deponent and active in meaning: she did not judge it beneath her. magni is separated from its noun Iovis by five words and the line-end at 585/586, so the greatness of Jupiter arrives only after the kneeling. The one verb governs both infinitives, procumbere and addere.

sentences.t:
“Omnibus inferior, quas sustinet aureus aether
(nam mihi sunt totum rarissima templa per orbem),
diva tamen veni, non ut delubra diesque
des mihi sacrificos caliturasque ignibus aras.
sentences.l: “Inferior to all the goddesses whom the golden upper air holds up (for temples of mine are the fewest through the whole world), yet a goddess I have come, not so that you may give me shrines and sacrificial days and altars that will grow hot with fires.
sentences.i: “The least of all the goddesses the golden sky holds up — for temples of mine are the scarcest the world over — still, I have come as a goddess, and not so that you should give me shrines, or feast days, or altars warm with sacrificial fire.
sentences.n: omnibus is an ablative of comparison after the comparative inferior, “lower than all of them”, and quas shows the understood noun is feminine: the other goddesses. mihi sunt … templa is the dative of possession, “temples are to me”, which is how Latin says “I have temples”. veni is the perfect vēnī, “I have come”. Scanned foot by foot the line runs dī-vă-tă | mēn-vē | nī-nōn | ūt-dē | lū-bră-dĭ | ēs-quĕ; the second foot mēn-vē is a spondee, so the e of veni is long, and that is the perfect vēnī and not the imperative vĕnī, “come”, whose e is short — both forms end in a long ī, so the third foot settles nothing. In the fourth foot ut is heavy because its t closes the syllable before the d of delubra. non ut … des is a purpose clause with the subjunctive: she says at once what she has not come for. caliturasque is a future participle, altars that are going to grow hot; the three refused gifts are delubra, dies and arae, and totum … per orbem is wrapped around rarissima templa.

sentences.l: Yet should you look at how much I, a woman, render to you, at the time when with new light I keep the borders of night, you would think that rewards must be given;
sentences.i: Yet if you would only consider how much I, a woman, do for you, at the hour when I hold the frontier of night with new light, you would judge that a reward was owed;
sentences.n: adspicias and putes are both present subjunctive: the condition is put as a supposition, “should you look … you would think”, not as a fact. quantum … praestem is an indirect question, which is why praestem is subjunctive too; praesto with the dative tibi is the verb for rendering a service. femina is in apposition to the “I” inside praestem — she presses the point that a female divinity does this work. noctis confinia is the border where night ends, the post she keeps with luce nova. danda is a gerundive: what must be given. The edition prints adspicias with adsp-, not asp-, and that spelling is kept.

sentences.t:
sed non ea cura neque hic est
nunc status Aurorae, meritos ut poscat honores:
sentences.l: but that is not the care, nor is this now the standing of Aurora, that she should demand the honours she has earned:
sentences.i: but that is not what is at issue, and Aurora is in no condition now to be claiming the honours she has earned:
sentences.n: Aurora is inside her own speech here and names herself in the third person, Aurorae … poscat, as if reporting on someone else — the distance is part of the plea. ea cura and hic status are two nominatives sharing one est. hic is cut off from its noun status by the line-end at 593/594. The ut clause is one of result reaching back to non ea … neque hic: her state is not such that she should be asking for anything. meritos … honores is wrapped around ut poscat, and meritos means earned, not merely deserved in the abstract.

sentences.t:
Memnonis orba mei venio, qui fortia frustra
pro patruo tulit arma suo primisque sub annis
occidit a forti, sic vos voluistis, Achille.
sentences.l: Bereft of my Memnon I come, who in vain bore brave arms for his uncle, and in his earliest years fell by brave — so you willed it — Achilles.
sentences.i: I come robbed of my Memnon, who took up brave arms for his uncle to no purpose, and in his first youth went down before brave Achilles — that was your will.
sentences.n: orba takes the genitive of what one is bereft of, and Memnonis is split from its adjective mei by orba itself, so the loss stands between the name and the word “my”. patruus is the father's brother in particular, not any uncle: Memnon is fighting for Troy through his father's line. fortia is held back from arma by the line-end at 595/596, and patruo from suo by tulit arma. occidit is active, “he fell”, yet it takes an agent phrase with a and the ablative, a forti … Achille, the construction a verb of being killed would take. Between that adjective and its noun Ovid wedges the whole parenthesis sic vos voluistis, addressed to the gods in the plural, so that “brave” and “Achilles” stand on either side of the gods' decision.

sentences.t:
Da, precor, huic aliquem, solacia mortis, honorem,
summe deum rector, maternaque vulnera leni.”
sentences.l: Give, I pray, to him some honour — consolations for his death — highest ruler of the gods, and soothe a mother's wounds.”
sentences.i: Grant him some honour, I beg you, to console his death, highest ruler of the gods, and soothe a mother's wounds.”
sentences.n: The prayer is framed by two imperatives, da opening 598 and leni closing 599. aliquem is separated from honorem by the whole phrase solacia mortis, which is a plural standing in apposition to the singular honorem: the one honour is to serve as consolations. deum is the shortened genitive plural for deorum, normal in this vocative formula. materna vulnera are the mother's own wounds, not her son's — she asks for a dressing on her grief, and leni is the verb for soothing a hurt.

sentences.t:
Iuppiter adnuerat, cum Memnonis arduus alto
corruit igne rogus nigrique volumine fumi
infecere diem (veluti cum flumina natas
exhalant nebulas, nec sol admittitur infra);
sentences.l: Jupiter had nodded assent, when Memnon's steep pyre collapsed in deep fire, and with a rolling mass of black smoke they stained the day (just as when rivers breathe out the mists born of them, and the sun is not admitted below);
sentences.i: Jupiter had given his nod, when Memnon's high pyre fell in with its deep fire, and with a rolling of black smoke they darkened the day (as when rivers breathe out the mists born of them, and the sun is not let through below);
sentences.n: adnuerat is pluperfect and the cum clause carries the action rather than the setting: “Jupiter had nodded, when …”. The nod is the god's own gesture of assent. arduus is cut from rogus and alto from igne across the line-end at 600/601, the two pairs interlocking. infecere is infecerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect in -ere, which returns at sonuere (608) and meminere (616) — but here there is nothing plural for it to agree with: Magnus prints volumine, an ablative singular, so “with a rolling mass of black smoke” cannot be the subject, and the verb is left without an expressed nominative. Some editions print volumina, which makes “the coils of black smoke” the subject of infecere. The text is given as printed, and the literal can only put in an English “they” for a subject the Latin never names. In the simile natas is from nascor, a deponent and active in meaning, “the mists born of them”; Magnus prints flumina natas exhalant nebulas, where some editions read flumine Nais exhalat and make a water-nymph the one who breathes them out.

sentences.t:
atra favilla volat glomerataque corpus in unum
densetur faciemque capit sumitque calorem
atque animam ex igni (levitas sua praebuit alas),
sentences.l: The black ash flies, and, balled into one body, it is packed tight and takes a shape and takes heat and life from the fire (its own lightness supplied wings),
sentences.i: The black ash flies up and, rolled together into a single body, thickens, takes on a shape, draws heat and breath from the fire — its own lightness gave it wings —
sentences.n: One singular subject, favilla, is carried through a chain of verbs — volat, densetur, capit, sumit — and the change happens between them rather than in any one of them. glomerata is a perfect participle, “having been balled up”, and densetur is passive: the ash is packed tight, not packing anything. corpus in unum is “into one body”, the mass before it has a shape; faciem is then the shape it takes. animam is breath and life at once. The edition prints the ablative igni rather than igne. The parenthesis is an aside in the poet's own voice, and its perfect praebuit steps out of the present tense around it: sua refers back to the ash, its own lightness.

sentences.t:
et primo similis volucri, mox vera volucris
insonuit pennis:
sentences.l: and at first like a bird, soon a true bird, it sounded with its wings:
sentences.i: and at first resembling a bird, then a bird in truth, it set up a noise with its wings:
sentences.n: similis takes the dative, so volucri is “like a bird”, while volucris a few words later is nominative, “a bird”, the thing itself: the same word in two cases marks the moment the likeness becomes the fact, and primo … mox measures the interval. insonuit is “sounded, made a noise”, with pennis as the ablative of the means — the noise is the beating of the feathers, the first thing the new creature does.

sentences.t:
pariter sonuere sorores
innumerae, quibus est eadem natalis origo,
terque rogum lustrant, et consonus exit in auras
ter plangor:
sentences.l: at the same moment countless sisters sounded, who have one and the same origin of birth, and three times they circle the pyre, and three times a wailing sounding in unison goes out into the air:
sentences.i: and with it countless sisters sounded together, all sprung from the same birth, and three times they ring the pyre, and three times a wail in unison goes up into the air:
sentences.n: sonuere is sonuerunt again, the same third-plural perfect met at infecere. quibus est … origo is the dative of possession: “to whom there is the same birth-origin”, that is, they all come out of the one pyre. The tense then slips from the perfect sonuere into the present lustrant and exit — the historic present, which brings the circling up close and holds it there. lustro is the verb for going ceremonially round a thing, so the three circuits are a funeral rite, not mere flying; terque at 610 and ter at 611 put the count twice. plangor is the noise of beating the breast in mourning, and consonus is separated from it by the line-end at 610/611, so “sounding together” arrives before the reader knows what sounds.

sentences.t: quarto seducunt castra volatu.
sentences.l: at a fourth flight they draw their camps apart.
sentences.i: on the fourth circuit they draw apart into two camps.
sentences.n: quarto and volatu sit at the two ends of the clause with the verb and its object between them; the ablative volatu counts the circuit, following the ter … ter of the line before, and the fourth breaks the ritual three. castra is the military word for a camp, and seduco is to lead apart: the mourning flock divides itself into two war-camps, which is where the language of the passage turns from funeral rite to campaign.

sentences.t:
Tam duo diversa populi de parte feroces
bella gerunt rostrisque et aduncis unguibus iras
exercent alasque adversaque pectora iactant
sentences.l: So fierce, two hosts from an opposite quarter wage wars, and with beaks and with hooked claws they ply their angers and fling their wings and their breasts set against each other
sentences.i: So two fierce hosts, from opposite quarters, make war, working off their rage with beak and hooked claw, flinging wings and breasts against each other
sentences.n: Magnus prints Tam, “so [fierce]”, with no correlative clause to answer it; some editions print tum, “then”, which is easier. duo is the masculine form — the feminine would be duae — so it cannot agree with the sisters; the masculine noun it counts is populi, nominative plural, “two hosts”, with diversa … de parte standing between the two words. (populi can also be taken as a genitive singular inside that phrase, “from a different quarter of the flock”, and then duo is left standing alone with its noun understood.) populus is a word for a people, used here of the birds, and the vocabulary around it is all military: bella gerunt, iras exercent, adversa pectora, after the castra of the line before. iras is plural, separate bursts of rage rather than one. The sentence runs on into the next unit: 612 to 616 carry no internal punctuation at all in the edition, and the break here falls at the line-end after iactant.

sentences.t:
inferiaeque cadunt cineri cognata sepulto
corpora seque viro forti meminere creatas.
sentences.l: and as offerings to the dead kindred bodies fall to the buried ash, and they remembered themselves begotten of a brave man.
sentences.i: and kindred bodies fall as grave-offerings on the buried ashes, and they remembered that a brave man had fathered them.
sentences.n: The word order interlocks twice over: cineri is separated from sepulto by cognata, and cognata from corpora by the line-end at 615/616, so the buried ash and the kindred bodies are laced through each other. inferiae is a nominative standing predicatively — the bodies fall as the offerings owed to the dead, so the birds are both mourners and sacrifice. se … creatas is an accusative with infinitive after meminere, with esse left out; creatas is feminine, agreeing with the sorores. meminere is meminerunt, the third-plural perfect again, and it stands beside the present cadunt in the same sentence. fortis has now been used of Memnon's arms (595), of the Achilles who killed him (597), and here of Memnon himself.

sentences.t: praepetibus subitis nomen facit auctor:
sentences.l: For the birds that are suddenly there, their originator makes the name:
sentences.i: Their originator gives these sudden birds their name:
sentences.n: praepes is a bird of swift flight, the word used of birds watched for omens, and subitis says only that they are suddenly there. nomen facit takes the dative of the person the name is made for. auctor is the originator, the one the birds come from — Memnon, whose ash they are. Line 616 ends in a full stop and Magnus nevertheless prints praepetibus with a small initial at the head of 617; every other sentence-opening after a full stop in this part is capitalised — Cura, At, Si, Da, Iuppiter, Tam, Ergo. The small p is given as printed, not corrected.

sentences.t:
ab illo
Memnonides dictae, cum sol duodena peregit
signa, parentali moriturae voce rebellant.
sentences.l: from him they were called Memnonides; when the sun has run through the twelve signs, with the voice of the rite for the dead, about to die, they make war again.
sentences.i: after him they are called the Memnonides; and whenever the sun has run through all twelve signs, with the cry of the rites for the dead, and doomed to die, they fight the battle over again.
sentences.n: dictae stands without sunt, which the reader supplies; with it the verb is a perfect passive, “they were named”, though the name is still theirs, which is why the idiomatic says “are called”. duodena is a distributive numeral used for the plain twelve, and the twelve signs are the sun's year, so the cum clause fixes the anniversary. moriturae is a future participle, feminine plural: they are already the ones who are going to die when they begin. parentali voce is the voice of the rites owed to a dead kinsman; Magnus prints voce, some editions more, “after the manner of the rites”. rebello is to renew a war that was already fought, so the annual battle repeats the one at the pyre rather than starting a new one.

sentences.t: Ergo aliis latrasse Dymantida flebile visum est:
sentences.l: So to others it seemed a thing for tears that the daughter of Dymas had barked:
sentences.i: So others found it a matter for tears that the daughter of Dymas had barked:
sentences.n: visum est is impersonal — it seemed so — with the accusative and infinitive Dymantida latrasse standing as what seemed, and flebile the neuter predicate, a thing to be wept over. latrasse is the shortened form of latravisse. Dymantida keeps its Greek ending, the accusative of a patronymic: the daughter of Dymas, that is the Hecuba named at 577, whose barking is what the others weep at. aliis, “to others”, is set against Aurora in the next unit: the pivot of the whole close is that other people's grief is not hers.

sentences.t:
luctibus est Aurora suis intenta, piasque
nunc quoque dat lacrimas et toto rorat in orbe.
sentences.l: Aurora is intent upon griefs of her own, and now too she gives dutiful tears and drips with dew over the whole world.
sentences.i: Aurora is taken up with a grief of her own: to this day she gives her dutiful tears, and drips dew the whole world over.
sentences.n: intenta takes the dative luctibus, and suis marks them off as her own against the aliis of the line before. quoque here is the plain adverb, “now too”, not the quo-que that means “and with which”; nunc quoque brings the story down to the reader's own morning. pias is the adjective for duty owed to one's kin, so the tears are an offering still being paid, and it is held back from lacrimas by the line-end at 621/622. rorat is intransitive, “she is wet with dew, she drips dew”, and toto … in orbe is wrapped around it: the morning dew anywhere is her weeping.
